## What you'll build
 
In this workshop, you'll take an AI agent that answers questions about a knowledge graph — and give it memory.
 
The memory comes from `neo4j-agent-memory`, a Python package from Neo4j Labs. It gives an agent three layers of
memory, stored together in one Neo4j graph.
 
You'll run a finished memory agent first, then build your own from the same starting point, layer by layer, until the two
match.

# workshop-agent-memory: An Agent That Forgets
 
## Three gaps
 
An agent without memory has three gaps, and you'll feel each of them close in this workshop:
 
* **No memory:** Ask it about last week's conversation and it starts from zero, every time. This one closes in the next
few minutes.
* **No record of reasoning:** When something goes wrong, nothing can explain why the agent decided what it did. This
one closes when you give your agent reasoning memory.
* **No shared learning:** Two agents

did. This
one closes when you give your agent reasoning memory.
* **No shared learning:** Two agents can't use what the other has learned. The shared workspace from your quickstart
closes this one before the module is out.

While the agent runs, the conversation lives in the running process, so it can follow along within a single session.

## Three layers of memory
 
Those functions write into three memory layers, all in the same Neo4j graph:
 
* **Short-term:** The conversation, message by message. It answers "what was discussed?"
* **Long-term:** What the agent learns about you - people, facts, and preferences.

* **Reasoning:** Why the agent answered as it did, step by step. It answers "how did you reach that conclusion?"
 
`get_context` reads across all three at once.
 
Together, they are why the agent could recall your name after a restart.

You have felt the difference: the same agent, forgetful one moment and persistent the next, with memory as the only
change.
 
The three layers are not separate stores. They live in one graph, and they connect - a message links out to the entities it
mentions, and a reasoning trace points back to the message that prompted it.
